title: Dividends
concept: A dividend is a payment a company may choose to make to shareholders using part of its profits or available cash.
learningObjective: Understand that distributing dividends is one of several ways a company may use its profits.
primaryMisconception: Every profitable company must pay dividends to its shareholders.
secondaryMisconceptions: A company that does not pay dividends is automatically performing badly.
Dividend payments are guaranteed and always remain the same.
keyTakeaway: A dividend is one possible way a company shares profit with shareholders.

screens.title: Profit Made—What Happens Next?
screens.content: A company earns £10,000. Must it pay shareholders, or could the money help the business in other ways?
screens.illustration: A £10,000 profit card stands at a crossroads with four hidden paths.

screens.title: A Successful Year
screens.content: BrightByte finishes the year with £10,000 available after its normal business costs. Its leaders must decide what to do next.
screens.illustration: A fictional technology company displays a £10,000 available-money card beside a decision table.

screens.title: Four Possible Uses
screens.content: The company could improve its products, keep money for future needs, repay debt, or give some money to eligible shareholders.
screens.illustration: Four cards show product development, a cash reserve, debt repayment, and shareholder payments.

screens.title: Is a Payment Required?
screens.content: Shareholder Zara owns five shares. She wonders whether earning a profit means BrightByte must send her money.
screens.illustration: Zara holds five share cards while a dividend envelope displays a question mark.

screens.title: What Must the Company Do?
screens.question: BrightByte earned a profit. Which statement is most accurate?

options.response: A profitable company may pay dividends, but it can also use the money in other ways.

options.text: It must keep all the money
options.response: Keeping a reserve is one option, but it is not the only possible decision.

options.text: It can choose among several uses
options.response: Correct. The company may reinvest, save, repay debt, or distribute part of the money.

options.text: Profit guarantees the same dividend every year
options.response: Dividend amounts may increase, decrease, remain unchanged, or stop.

screens.title: Where Can the Profit Go?
screens.instruction: Connect each company decision with its possible result. Then calculate what different shareholders may receive.

educationalAssumptions: The activity treats £10,000 as money available after normal operating costs.
Real accounting profit and available cash are not always the same.
The company has several possible uses for the money.
Reinvestment may support growth but does not guarantee success.
Debt repayment may reduce future interest costs, depending on the debt terms.
The dividend example uses one ordinary share class with equal payments per eligible share.
Taxes, fees, different share classes, and other company commitments are excluded.
The activity does not recommend buying any real company’s shares.

effects.title: Support future growth
effects.content: The company may improve products, hire employees, open locations, or expand operations.

effects.title: Build a cash reserve
effects.content: The company keeps money available for future opportunities or unexpected costs.

effects.title: Reduce money owed
effects.content: The company lowers its outstanding debt and may reduce future interest costs.

effects.title: Pay eligible shareholders
effects.content: Eligible shareholders receive a payment based on the number of shares they own.

correctConnections.explanation: The company uses the money inside the business. This may help it grow, but success is not guaranteed.
The company keeps money available for future plans or unexpected costs.
Repaying debt lowers the outstanding balance and may reduce future interest costs.
The company shares some money with eligible shareholders according to the dividend declared per share.

incorrectConnectionFeedback.feedback: A reserve remains available as savings. Reinvestment puts the money into business activities.
Reinvestment funds company operations or growth rather than directly reducing debt.
Reinvested money stays inside the company rather than being distributed to shareholders.
Saving the money builds a reserve. Expansion would require the company to use or reinvest it.
Money kept as savings remains available rather than being used to repay what the company owes.
Money distributed to shareholders leaves the company instead of remaining in its reserve.
Debt repayment reduces money owed rather than directly funding new products or locations.
Money used to repay debt is no longer being kept as available savings.
Debt repayment goes to lenders. Dividends are paid to eligible shareholders.
Dividend money is distributed to shareholders rather than reinvested in the company.
A dividend reduces cash held by the company instead of building its reserve.
Dividends go to eligible shareholders, while debt repayments go to lenders.

dividendExample.disclaimer: This is a fictional classroom example, not a promised or predicted payment.

followUpQuestions.scenario: Zara owns 5 shares and the dividend is £1 per eligible share.
followUpQuestions.question: How much does Zara receive?
followUpQuestions.explanation: Zara receives £1 for each of her five eligible shares.

followUpQuestions.scenario: Noah owns 20 shares and the dividend is £1 per eligible share.
followUpQuestions.question: How much does Noah receive?
followUpQuestions.explanation: Noah receives £1 for each of his twenty eligible shares.

followUpQuestions.scenario: Maya owns 0 shares and the dividend is £1 per eligible share.
followUpQuestions.question: How much does Maya receive?
followUpQuestions.explanation: A person who owns no eligible shares receives no dividend.

followUpQuestions.scenario: BrightByte earns another profit next year.
followUpQuestions.question: Must it pay the same £1 dividend again?

options.text: Yes, profitable companies must repeat dividends
No, the company may change or stop the dividend
No, because companies can pay only once

followUpQuestions.explanation: Future dividends depend on company decisions, available cash, plans, obligations, and business conditions.

simplificationExplanation: This activity shows four common choices separately.
A real company may divide its available money across several uses.
A company might reinvest some money, repay some debt, keep a reserve, and distribute only part as a dividend.
A company can earn an accounting profit without having the same amount available as cash.

screens.title: One Choice Among Several
screens.content: You connected company profit with four possible uses. A dividend is a payment a company may choose to make to eligible shareholders, often stated as an amount per share. A profitable company does not have to pay one. It may reinvest, build savings, or repay debt instead. A company can also split its money between several choices. Dividends may increase, decrease, remain unchanged, or stop, so shareholders should never treat them as guaranteed income.
screens.simpleSummary: A dividend is optional and depends on the company’s decision.
screens.illustration: A company-profit card divides across growth, savings, debt, and dividend paths, with no path marked as compulsory.

screens.title: The Clothing Brand’s Decision
screens.content: A fictional clothing brand earns money from a successful launch. Instead of paying a dividend, it keeps part as savings and uses the rest to improve its website. The lack of a dividend does not automatically mean the company performed badly.
screens.illustration: Profit from clothing sales divides between a savings reserve and a website-upgrade card.

questions.text: A company declares a dividend of £0.50 per share. Liam owns eight eligible shares. How much does he receive?

options.feedback: £0.50 is the payment for one share. Liam owns eight shares.
Four shares would receive £2. Eight shares receive twice that amount.
Correct. Eight shares multiplied by £0.50 equals £4.
£8 would mean a dividend of £1 per share rather than £0.50.

questions.correctExplanation: Eight shares multiplied by £0.50 per share equals £4.
questions.misconceptionTested: A dividend payment is unrelated to the number of eligible shares owned.

questions.text: A profitable company pays no dividend and uses the money to develop a new product. What does this show?

options.text: Profitable companies may choose to reinvest instead
options.feedback: Correct. A dividend is optional, and reinvestment may support the company’s plans.
A profitable company may intentionally keep or reinvest money to support future plans.

options.text: Every shareholder has lost their shares
options.feedback: Not receiving a dividend does not remove the shareholder’s ownership.
Companies are not automatically required to distribute dividends whenever they earn a profit.

questions.correctExplanation: A dividend is optional. A company may decide that investing in its operations is a better use of the money.
questions.misconceptionTested: Every profitable company must pay dividends to its shareholders.

questions.text: A company paid £1 per share last year. What should shareholders expect this year?

options.text: The dividend could rise, fall, stay the same, or stop
options.feedback: Correct. A previous dividend does not guarantee the next payment.
A previous dividend does not guarantee the same future payment.
Dividend payments can increase, but they can also decrease or stop.
The company may choose to use its profit in other ways.

questions.correctExplanation: Dividend decisions can change with the company’s available cash, plans, obligations, and business conditions.
questions.misconceptionTested: Dividend payments are guaranteed and always remain the same.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on dividends as one possible use of company profits or available cash.
The mission distinguishes profit from available cash, explains per-share payments, and presents dividends as optional and changeable.
The mission uses fictional companies, straightforward calculations, business choices, and introductory shareholder concepts suitable for teens.
The mission does not recommend buying any real dividend-paying company or investment.
The mission states that dividend payments may increase, decrease, remain unchanged, or stop.
The mission does not predict the future price of any stock or company.
Companies and shareholders are discussed neutrally whether dividends are paid or not.
The mission clarifies that profit and cash differ, companies may combine several uses, and dividends depend on company decisions and eligibility.
The mission uses pounds, technology and clothing companies, shares, debt, savings, and familiar business decisions for UK teens.
The learner connects four company decisions with their effects and calculates shareholder payments.
The quiz addresses mandatory dividends, companies that reinvest profits, per-share calculations, and changing future payments.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, four cause-and-effect connections, four interaction questions, and three concise quiz questions.
